Hagiasmos
hah-gee-as-MOS
n. (Greek)
Greek hagiasmos, “sanctification, holiness,” from hagiazō (to make holy, sanctify), from hagios (holy). Both the act of sanctification and the resulting state of holiness.

📖 Biblical Definition

Hagiasmos is the New Testament’s precise word for sanctification—both the act by which God sets His people apart and progressively conforms them to His holiness, and the resulting state of holiness in the redeemed. The word stands at the heart of one of the great structural doctrines of Reformed theology: the distinction-and-relation between justification (the legal declaration of righteousness through faith in Christ) and sanctification (the moral transformation of the believer by the Spirit). Both are works of God; both are received by faith; both are anchored in union with Christ; neither can be collapsed into the other; neither can be separated from the other. Paul ties them together in 1 Corinthians 6:11: and such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God. Sanctification has both a definitive moment (the believer is set apart at conversion, called saints [hagioi, holy ones] across the NT from that moment onward) and a progressive course (the believer is being progressively conformed to the image of Christ across his Christian life). 1 Thessalonians 4:3 sets the will of God explicitly: for this is the will of God, even your sanctification. Hebrews 12:14: follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord. 2 Corinthians 7:1: let us cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God. The means of sanctification are several. The Word: sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth (John 17:17). The Spirit: through sanctification of the Spirit (2 Thess 2:13; 1 Pet 1:2). Providential dealing: whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth (Heb 12:6). The means of grace (Word, sacraments, prayer, gathering). The saint’s active cooperation: work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure (Phil 2:12-13)—divine working and human working, each in its proper relation. The eschatological end of sanctification is the perfect conformity to Christ at His appearing: we know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). Sanctification is therefore the long arc of the believer’s being made holy as the Holy One who has set him apart is holy—a work begun at conversion, sustained across the Christian life, and consummated at the resurrection in the perfect likeness of Christ.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

(Greek term.) Hagiasmos: sanctification, holiness; both the act of being set apart unto God and the progressive moral transformation of the believer toward the image of Christ; structural doctrine of Reformed theology, distinguished from justification but inseparable from it.

SANCTIFICATION, n. — 1. The act of God’s grace by which the affections of men are purified or alienated from sin and the world, and exalted to a supreme love to God. 2. The act of consecrating or of setting apart for a sacred purpose. 3. The state of being sanctified; the state of being holy and devoted to God.

HAGIASMOS — (Greek noun, G38.) Sanctification, holiness. 10 NT uses (Rom 6:19, 22; 1 Cor 1:30; 1 Thess 4:3, 4, 7; 2 Thess 2:13; 1 Tim 2:15; Heb 12:14; 1 Pet 1:2). The progressive work of the Spirit conforming the believer to the image of Christ.

📖 Key Scripture

1 Thessalonians 4:3 — "For this is the will of God, even your sanctification, that ye should abstain from fornication."

Hebrews 12:14 — "Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord."

2 Thessalonians 2:13 — "But we are bound to give thanks alway to God for you, brethren beloved of the Lord, because God hath from the beginning chosen you to salvation through sanctification of the Spirit and belief of the truth."

1 Corinthians 6:11 — "And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Hagiasmos-shaped sanctification is corrupted, on one side, by the antinomian-grace tradition that has separated sanctification from the gospel and treated it as an optional addition to a justification-only salvation—and on the other by the perfectionist traditions that have collapsed sanctification’s long progressive course into a single decisive crisis-experience producing complete sinlessness in this life.

expand to see more

The antinomian-grace tradition has separated sanctification from the gospel and treated it as an optional addition to a justification-only salvation. On this account, the believer is justified by faith in Christ, declared righteous, and need not concern himself unduly with the progressive moral transformation toward holiness that the New Testament uniformly assumes will follow. The result is a gospel-claim without any gospel-life: claims of conversion paired with patterns of life that show no progressive sanctification, doctrinal precision divorced from any visible holiness, profession without the corresponding moral transformation the Spirit produces in every regenerate saint. Scripture refuses the separation. Justification and sanctification are distinct gifts but never separable; the Christ who justifies also sanctifies; the Spirit who applies the imputed righteousness of Christ to the believer also indwells him and progressively conforms him to Christ’s image. The recovery is the integrated doctrine: salvation is a Christ-given complex of justification, sanctification, and glorification, in which the believer is declared righteous, progressively made holy, and at last fully conformed to Christ—all gifts of grace, all received by faith, all in their proper distinction-and-relation.

The opposite corruption is the perfectionist tradition that has collapsed sanctification’s long progressive course into a single decisive crisis-experience producing complete sinlessness in this life. Various Wesleyan, Holiness, and Keswick traditions have taught versions of this: a second blessing, an entire sanctification, a complete consecration that eradicates indwelling sin and produces sinless Christian perfection in the present. Scripture refuses this also. 1 John 1:8: if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us; the saint sins, confesses, is forgiven, is being progressively sanctified, and will be fully conformed only at the resurrection. Sanctification is progressive across the Christian life, with seasons of more visible progress and seasons of struggle, but does not reach perfection in this present age. Recover both ends. Refuse the antinomian separation of sanctification from the gospel, and refuse the perfectionist collapse of progressive sanctification into a single crisis-experience. The biblical pattern is the long, Spirit-wrought, progressive conformity of the saint to the image of Christ—begun at conversion, sustained across the Christian life through the appointed means of grace, and consummated only at the resurrection in the perfect likeness of the Lord.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek hagiasmos (sanctification, holiness), from hagiazō (to make holy) from hagios (holy)—the act and state of being set apart unto God and progressively conformed to His holiness; structural doctrine of Reformed theology, distinguished from justification but inseparable from it, by the means of Word, Spirit, providence, and means of grace.

expand to see more

Greek hagiasmos (G38) — sanctification, holiness (Rom 6:19, 22; 1 Cor 1:30; 1 Thess 4:3, 4, 7; 2 Thess 2:13; 1 Tim 2:15; Heb 12:14; 1 Pet 1:2).

Greek hagiazō (G37) — to make holy, sanctify, set apart (28 NT uses).

Greek hagios (G40) — holy (over 230 NT uses; the great holiness-adjective applied to God, things, places, days, and saints).

Greek hagiōsunē (G42) — holiness (Rom 1:4; 2 Cor 7:1; 1 Thess 3:13).

Usage

"For this is the will of God, even your sanctification—1 Thess 4:3 sets sanctification as the explicit will of God for every believer."

"Justification and sanctification are distinct gifts but never separable: the Christ who justifies also sanctifies; the Spirit who applies imputed righteousness also indwells and progressively conforms."

"Antinomianism separates sanctification from the gospel; perfectionism collapses its long course into a crisis-experience; biblical hagiasmos is the long Spirit-wrought progressive conformity of the saint to Christ, consummated only at the resurrection."
